stories.title: The First World War
stories.blurb: How did a shooting in Sarajevo become a four-year war that killed millions and broke four empires?

steps.name: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
steps.what: Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb student, shot the heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne and his wife Sophie as their car stopped on a Sarajevo street.
steps.why: Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia set off a chain of alliance mobilisations that brought Russia, Germany, France and Britain into war by early August.

steps.name: First Battle of the Marne
steps.what: French and British armies counter-attacked the German advance about 50 km from Paris and forced it back to the Aisne river.
steps.why: The German plan for a quick victory in the west failed, and both sides dug the trench lines that would barely move for four years.

steps.name: Christmas truce
steps.what: Along parts of the Western Front, British and German soldiers stopped firing, sang carols, buried their dead and met in no man's land.
steps.why: It showed how ordinary soldiers saw the enemy, and commanders made sure it was not repeated on that scale.

steps.name: Armenian genocide
steps.what: Ottoman authorities arrested about 235 to 270 Armenian community leaders in Constantinople, beginning deportations and massacres that killed most of the Ottoman Armenian population.
steps.why: The war gave cover for the destruction of a whole people, one of the first modern genocides.

steps.name: Gallipoli campaign
steps.what: British, French, Australian and New Zealand troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula to open the Dardanelles but were held by Ottoman forces and withdrew after about eight months.
steps.why: The failure kept the sea route to Russia closed and made Mustafa Kemal's name as a commander.

steps.name: Sinking of the RMS Lusitania
steps.place_name: Off the Old Head of Kinsale, Ireland
steps.what: The German submarine U-20 torpedoed the British liner Lusitania, killing 1,197 people, 128 of them Americans.
steps.why: U-boat attacks on shipping turned American opinion against Germany long before the United States entered the war.

steps.name: Battle of Verdun
steps.what: Germany attacked the fortress city of Verdun; over ten months the French held it at the cost of roughly 300,000 dead on both sides.
steps.why: It became the model of attrition warfare, where the aim was to bleed the enemy rather than to win ground.

steps.name: Battle of Jutland
steps.what: About 250 British and German warships fought the war's largest naval battle; Britain lost more ships, but the German fleet returned to port.
steps.why: The German surface fleet never seriously challenged the British blockade again, pushing Germany towards submarine warfare.

steps.name: Battle of the Somme
steps.what: The British army lost about 57,000 casualties on the first day alone; by November the Allies had advanced about 10 km for over a million casualties on both sides.
steps.why: It came to stand for the human cost of trench warfare and also saw the first use of tanks in battle.

steps.name: Turnip Winter
steps.what: After a failed potato harvest and under the British blockade, German city dwellers lived largely on turnips, normally animal feed, and civilian deaths from hunger and disease rose.
steps.why: Hunger at home wore down German morale and fed the unrest that ended the empire in 1918.

steps.name: American entry into World War I
steps.what: After Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on 1 February and the Zimmermann Telegram was published, Congress declared war on Germany.
steps.why: American men, money and supplies shifted the balance against Germany in 1918.
steps.wikipedia: American entry into World War I

steps.name: Battle of Caporetto
steps.what: Austro-Hungarian and German troops broke the Italian line on the Isonzo and drove the Italians back about 100 km to the Piave, taking some 265,000 prisoners.
steps.why: The near collapse of Italy led the Allies to create a unified command structure.

steps.date_note: first widely recorded outbreak; the origin of the pandemic is disputed
steps.name: Spanish flu
steps.what: An influenza outbreak among army recruits in Kansas was among the first recorded cases of a pandemic that troopships spread worldwide and that killed perhaps 25 to 50 million people.
steps.why: The war's mass movements of soldiers helped spread a disease that killed more people than the fighting did.

steps.name: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
steps.what: Soviet Russia signed a separate peace with the Central Powers, giving up Poland, the Baltic lands, Finland and Ukraine.
steps.why: Germany could move dozens of divisions west for one last offensive in the spring of 1918.

steps.name: Armistice of 11 November 1918
steps.what: In a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne, German delegates signed an armistice that took effect at 11 a.m.
steps.why: The fighting ended with Germany's army still on foreign soil, which later fed the myth that it had been betrayed at home.

stories.title: The Russian revolutions
stories.blurb: How did the Romanov empire fall, and how did the Bolsheviks win the civil war that followed?

steps.date_note: 23 February in the Russian Old Style calendar
steps.name: February Revolution
steps.what: Women queuing for bread on International Women's Day began strikes that spread to over 200,000 workers; within days the garrison mutinied.
steps.why: War shortages turned bread riots into a revolution that ended three centuries of Romanov rule.

steps.name: Abdication of Nicholas II
steps.what: Stranded in his train at Pskov, Tsar Nicholas II signed his abdication for himself and his son.
steps.why: Power passed to a weak Provisional Government that shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet.

steps.name: Lenin's sealed train
steps.what: With German permission, Lenin and about 30 other exiles left Zurich in a train that crossed Germany, then went on by ferry and rail through Sweden and Finland.
steps.why: Germany helped bring home the leader most committed to taking Russia out of the war.

steps.name: April Theses
steps.what: Arriving at the Finland Station, Lenin called for no support to the Provisional Government and all power to the soviets.
steps.why: His programme turned the Bolsheviks from partners in the revolution into its rivals.

steps.date_note: 25 October in the Old Style calendar
steps.name: October Revolution
steps.what: Red Guards and soldiers led by the Bolsheviks seized Petrograd's key points and the Winter Palace, arresting the Provisional Government's ministers.
steps.why: It put the world's first communist party in power.

steps.name: Decree on Land
steps.what: The Congress of Soviets abolished private ownership of land and handed estates to peasant committees.
steps.why: It approved the land seizures peasants were already making and kept the countryside from turning against the new regime at first.

steps.name: Dissolution of the Russian Constituent Assembly
steps.what: The freely elected assembly, where the Socialist Revolutionaries had won the most seats, met for one day before the Bolsheviks closed it.
steps.why: It ended the hope of a multi-party Russia and pushed opponents towards armed resistance.

steps.name: Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
steps.what: The Soviet government made peace with Germany, giving up territory holding about a third of the old empire's population.
steps.why: Lenin traded land for time to hold power, and many Russians saw the treaty as a betrayal.

steps.name: Revolt of the Czechoslovak Legion
steps.what: About 40,000 Czech and Slovak soldiers travelling east along the Trans-Siberian Railway clashed with Soviet authorities and took control of much of the line.
steps.why: Their revolt opened the way for anti-Bolshevik governments across the Volga, Urals and Siberia.

steps.name: Execution of the Romanov family
steps.what: Bolshevik guards shot the former tsar, his wife, their five children and four servants in a cellar as White forces approached the city.
steps.why: It removed any rallying figure for a restored monarchy.

steps.name: Kolchak takes power in Omsk
steps.what: Admiral Alexander Kolchak took power in Omsk as Supreme Ruler of the White movement in Siberia.
steps.why: The Whites gained a single leader in the east, but their armies stayed divided and far apart.

steps.name: Battle of Warsaw (1920)
steps.what: Polish forces under Piłsudski counter-attacked the Red Army at the gates of Warsaw and drove it back east.
steps.why: It stopped the spread of the revolution into central Europe by force.

steps.name: Kronstadt rebellion
steps.what: Sailors at the Kronstadt naval base, once Bolshevik heroes, demanded free soviets and an end to grain requisitions; the Red Army crushed them across the ice.
steps.why: A revolt from the regime's own base showed that war communism had lost popular support.

steps.name: New Economic Policy
steps.what: The Tenth Party Congress replaced grain requisitioning with a tax in kind and let peasants and small traders sell for profit again.
steps.why: Lenin retreated to a partly market economy to rebuild a country ruined by seven years of war.
steps.date_note: tax in kind adopted at the Tenth Party Congress, 8-16 March

steps.name: Russian famine of 1921–1922
steps.what: Drought on top of years of requisitioning caused famine along the Volga that killed around five million people, despite American Relief Administration food aid.
steps.why: The famine was the civil war's final cost to ordinary peasants.

steps.name: Treaty on the Creation of the USSR
steps.what: Delegates of the Russian, Ukrainian, Belarusian and Transcaucasian soviet republics formally joined in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics.
steps.why: The Bolsheviks rebuilt most of the old empire as a federal communist state.
steps.wikipedia: Treaty on the Creation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics

stories.title: The road to the Second World War
stories.blurb: How did the peace of 1919 give way, step by step, to a second world war twenty years later?

steps.name: Treaty of Versailles
steps.what: Germany signed a peace that took about 13 percent of its territory, limited its army to 100,000 men and made it accept responsibility for the war and pay reparations.
steps.why: Many Germans saw the treaty as unjust, and overturning it became the aim of nationalist politics.

steps.name: March on Rome
steps.what: Thousands of Fascist blackshirts converged on Rome, and King Victor Emmanuel III invited Mussolini to form a government rather than resist.
steps.why: Fascism came to power and became a model for Hitler.

steps.name: Occupation of the Ruhr
steps.what: French and Belgian troops occupied Germany's industrial heartland after Germany fell behind on reparations; workers answered with passive resistance.
steps.why: The government printed money to pay striking workers, tipping inflation into collapse.

steps.name: Beer Hall Putsch
steps.what: Hitler and his Nazi Party tried to seize power in Munich; police fire killed 16 marchers and Hitler was later jailed, where he wrote Mein Kampf.
steps.why: The failure taught Hitler to seek power through elections rather than force.

steps.name: Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic
steps.what: By November one US dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks; on 15 November the new Rentenmark replaced the paper mark at one trillion to one.
steps.why: The wiping out of savings left the middle class bitter and distrustful of the republic.

steps.name: Wall Street crash of 1929
steps.what: Share prices on the New York exchange collapsed over a week of panic selling, from Black Thursday to Black Tuesday.
steps.why: The Great Depression that followed spread unemployment worldwide and helped extremists win votes, above all in Germany.

steps.name: Mukden incident
steps.what: Japanese officers set off a small bomb on a Japanese-owned railway and blamed China, using it as a pretext to occupy all of Manchuria.
steps.why: The League of Nations condemned Japan but did nothing, and Japan left the League in 1933.

steps.name: Hitler appointed chancellor
steps.what: President Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor; within months the Reichstag fire decree and the Enabling Act let him rule as a dictator.
steps.why: Germany came under a government set on overturning Versailles by force.

steps.name: Nuremberg Laws
steps.what: At the Nazi Party rally, the Reichstag passed laws stripping German Jews of citizenship and banning marriage between Jews and other Germans.
steps.why: Persecution of Jews became written law, a step on the road to genocide.

steps.name: Second Italo-Ethiopian War
steps.what: Italy invaded Ethiopia, using poison gas, and took Addis Ababa in May 1936; League sanctions left out oil.
steps.why: The League's failure to protect a member state showed aggressors they had little to fear.

steps.name: 1936 Summer Olympics
steps.what: Nazi Germany hosted the Olympic Games as a showcase, while the African American sprinter Jesse Owens won four gold medals.
steps.why: The regime used the Games to look peaceful and modern to the world while it rearmed.

steps.name: Bombing of Guernica
steps.what: During the Spanish Civil War, German Condor Legion and Italian aircraft bombed the Basque town of Guernica on market day, killing hundreds of civilians.
steps.why: Spain became a testing ground for the weapons and alliances of the coming war, and Picasso's painting made the raid a symbol.

steps.name: Anschluss
steps.what: German troops marched into Austria unopposed, and Hitler announced its union with Germany to crowds in Vienna three days later.
steps.why: Hitler broke Versailles openly and the Western powers only protested.

steps.name: Munich Agreement
steps.what: Britain, France and Italy agreed that Germany could annex the Sudetenland from Czechoslovakia, which was not invited to the talks.
steps.why: It became the textbook case of appeasement; in March 1939 Hitler took the rest of Czechoslovakia.

steps.name: Kristallnacht
steps.what: Nazi mobs burned over 1,000 synagogues and wrecked thousands of Jewish shops across Germany and Austria; about 30,000 Jewish men were sent to camps.
steps.why: The regime moved from legal discrimination to open state violence against Jews.

steps.name: Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact
steps.what: Germany and the Soviet Union signed a non-aggression pact with a secret protocol dividing Poland and eastern Europe between them.
steps.why: Freed from the risk of a two-front war, Hitler invaded Poland nine days later.

stories.title: The Second World War in Europe
stories.blurb: How did Germany conquer most of Europe, and how was it defeated from east and west?

steps.name: Invasion of Poland
steps.what: Germany invaded Poland, the Soviet Union attacked from the east on 17 September, and Poland was divided within five weeks.
steps.why: Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September, beginning the war in Europe.

steps.name: Dunkirk evacuation
steps.what: After the German breakthrough in France, warships and hundreds of small civilian boats carried about 338,000 British and French soldiers across the Channel.
steps.why: Britain saved its army to fight on, even as France fell.

steps.name: Armistice of 22 June 1940
steps.what: France signed an armistice in the same railway carriage used in 1918, leaving the north occupied and the south under the Vichy regime.
steps.why: Britain was left to fight Germany alone in the west.

steps.name: The Blitz
steps.what: The Luftwaffe bombed London on 57 nights in a row and then struck other cities, killing about 43,000 civilians; Londoners sheltered in Underground stations.
steps.why: The bombing failed to break British morale or to prepare an invasion.

steps.name: Operation Barbarossa
steps.what: About three million Axis soldiers invaded the Soviet Union along a front from the Baltic to the Black Sea.
steps.why: It opened the largest and deadliest theatre of the war, where most German soldiers would die.

steps.name: Siege of Leningrad
steps.what: German and Finnish forces cut off Leningrad for 872 days; bread rations fell to 125 grams a day and some 800,000 civilians died, mostly of starvation.
steps.why: Hunger was used as a weapon against a whole city, which was supplied only across frozen Lake Ladoga.

steps.name: Wannsee Conference
steps.what: Fifteen senior Nazi officials met in a lakeside villa to coordinate the deportation and murder of Europe's Jews.
steps.why: The killing already under way in the east became an organised continent-wide programme.

steps.name: Battle of Stalingrad
steps.what: After months of street fighting, a Soviet counter-offensive encircled the German Sixth Army, whose 91,000 survivors surrendered.
steps.why: It is widely seen as the turning point of the war in Europe.

steps.name: Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
steps.what: Jewish fighters with a few pistols and homemade bombs resisted the final deportation from the ghetto for almost a month.
steps.why: It was the largest Jewish revolt against the Holocaust.

steps.name: Battle of Kursk
steps.what: A German offensive against the Kursk salient broke on deep Soviet defences in one of the largest tank battles in history.
steps.why: After Kursk, Germany never again launched a major offensive in the east.

steps.name: Normandy landings
steps.what: About 156,000 American, British, Canadian and other Allied troops landed on five Normandy beaches on the first day.
steps.why: It opened the western front that Stalin had demanded since 1942.

steps.name: Operation Bagration
steps.what: The Red Army destroyed Germany's Army Group Centre in Belarus, freeing Minsk on 3 July and advancing to the Vistula.
steps.why: It was Germany's greatest defeat of the war and brought Soviet troops to Poland.

steps.name: Dutch famine of 1944–1945
steps.what: After a Dutch railway strike in September 1944, German restrictions on food transport and a hard winter brought famine to the western Netherlands, killing about 20,000.
steps.why: Civilians in occupied Europe paid for the war's last year in hunger.

steps.name: Liberation of Auschwitz
steps.what: Soviet soldiers reached Auschwitz and found about 7,000 prisoners left behind; around 1.1 million people, most of them Jews, had been murdered there.
steps.why: The largest Nazi death camp revealed the scale of the Holocaust.

steps.name: Battle of Berlin
steps.what: Soviet armies stormed Berlin; Hitler killed himself in his bunker on 30 April and the city surrendered on 2 May.
steps.why: Germany surrendered unconditionally on 8 May, ending the war in Europe.

stories.title: The Pacific war
stories.blurb: How did Japan's war in China grow into a Pacific war against the United States, and how did it end?

steps.name: Marco Polo Bridge incident
steps.what: A night clash between Japanese and Chinese troops at the Marco Polo Bridge grew into full-scale war within weeks.
steps.why: It began the Second Sino-Japanese War, which merged into the Second World War.

steps.name: Nanjing Massacre
steps.what: After taking China's capital, Japanese troops killed tens of thousands to perhaps 200,000 or more civilians and prisoners and raped many thousands of women.
steps.why: The massacre hardened Chinese resistance and remains a bitter issue between China and Japan.

steps.name: Burma Road
steps.what: About 200,000 Chinese labourers cut a road of over 1,100 km through mountains from Kunming to Lashio in British Burma, largely by hand.
steps.why: With its coast occupied, China depended on this road for outside supplies.

steps.name: Attack on Pearl Harbor
steps.what: Japanese carrier aircraft sank or damaged eight US battleships and killed about 2,400 Americans in a surprise attack.
steps.why: It brought the United States into the war against Japan, and Germany declared war on the US four days later.

steps.name: Fall of Singapore
steps.what: About 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops surrendered to a smaller Japanese army after a campaign of ten weeks.
steps.why: It was the largest British surrender in history and damaged European prestige across Asia.

steps.name: Battle of Midway
steps.place_name: North Pacific, northwest of Midway Atoll
steps.what: Forewarned by broken codes, US carrier aircraft sank four Japanese fleet carriers for the loss of one American carrier.
steps.why: Japan lost the naval initiative six months after Pearl Harbor.

steps.name: Guadalcanal campaign
steps.what: US Marines seized an unfinished Japanese airfield and held it through six months of land, sea and air battles until Japan withdrew.
steps.why: It was the first major Allied land offensive against Japan and began the long advance across the Pacific.

steps.date_note: work began at both ends in autumn 1942; some sources give June 1942
steps.name: Burma Railway
steps.what: Japan forced about 60,000 Allied prisoners and over 200,000 Asian labourers to build a 415 km railway from Thailand to Burma; some 12,000 prisoners and up to 90,000 Asian workers died.
steps.why: It shows the forced labour on which Japan's wartime empire relied.

steps.name: Bengal famine of 1943
steps.what: After the loss of Burmese rice imports, a cyclone and wartime price inflation, famine killed an estimated 2 to 3 million people in Bengal.
steps.why: War policies and slow official relief turned a food shortage into one of the century's worst famines.

steps.name: Battle of Leyte Gulf
steps.what: Covering MacArthur's return to the Philippines, the US Navy defeated the Japanese fleet in what may have been the largest naval battle in history; organised kamikaze attacks began here.
steps.why: The Japanese navy ceased to exist as a fighting force.

steps.name: Battle of Iwo Jima
steps.what: US Marines took the small volcanic island in five weeks; almost all of its 21,000 Japanese defenders and about 6,800 Americans were killed.
steps.why: The cost of each island fed American fears about invading Japan itself.

steps.name: Bombing of Tokyo (10 March 1945)
steps.what: Some 279 B-29 bombers dropped incendiaries on Tokyo's wooden districts at night, killing around 90,000 to 100,000 people and leaving over a million homeless.
steps.why: It was the deadliest single air raid of the war and began the firebombing of Japan's cities.

steps.name: Battle of Okinawa
steps.what: In the Pacific war's bloodiest battle, over 12,000 Americans, about 100,000 Japanese soldiers and a large share of Okinawa's civilians died.
steps.why: Okinawa was meant as the base for invading Japan's home islands.

steps.name: Atomic bombing of Hiroshima
steps.what: The B-29 Enola Gay dropped a uranium bomb on Hiroshima, killing about 70,000 to 80,000 people at once and many more by the end of the year.
steps.why: It was the first use of a nuclear weapon in war.
steps.wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

steps.name: Atomic bombing of Nagasaki
steps.what: A plutonium bomb destroyed much of Nagasaki, killing about 40,000 people at once, on the same day the Soviet Union invaded Manchuria.
steps.why: Together these shocks led Emperor Hirohito to accept surrender on 15 August.
steps.wikipedia: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

steps.name: Surrender of Japan
steps.what: Japanese representatives signed the instrument of surrender aboard the battleship Missouri in Tokyo Bay.
steps.why: The signing formally ended the Second World War.

stories.title: The partition of India
stories.blurb: Why did British India become two states in 1947, and why did it cost so many lives?

steps.name: Lahore Resolution
steps.what: The All-India Muslim League called for independent states in the Muslim-majority northwest and east of India.
steps.why: It made a separate Muslim homeland, Pakistan, the League's official goal.

steps.name: Cripps Mission
steps.what: Stafford Cripps offered dominion status after the war in return for Indian support, with a clause letting provinces opt out; Congress rejected it.
steps.why: The opt-out clause gave the idea of partition official standing for the first time.

steps.name: Quit India Movement
steps.what: Gandhi called on the British to quit India with the slogan 'Do or Die'; within hours the Congress leaders were arrested and held for most of the war.
steps.why: With Congress in jail, the Muslim League grew in strength while it cooperated with the British.

steps.name: Royal Indian Navy mutiny
steps.what: Indian sailors struck over pay, food and racism, and the strike spread to about 78 ships and 20,000 men before it was ended.
steps.why: Britain could no longer count on Indian armed forces to keep its rule.

steps.name: 1946 Cabinet Mission to India
steps.what: Three British cabinet ministers proposed a loose united India with groups of provinces; the plan collapsed over Congress and League distrust.
steps.why: It was the last serious attempt to keep India united.

steps.name: Direct Action Day
steps.what: A Muslim League protest day turned into the Great Calcutta Killings, in which about 4,000 Hindus and Muslims died in four days.
steps.why: Communal killing began to spread from city to city and made a peaceful united settlement seem impossible.

steps.name: Noakhali riots
steps.what: Attacks on Hindus in rural Noakhali were followed by Gandhi walking from village to village for four months to restore calm.
steps.why: Violence reached the countryside, and Gandhi's personal peace mission became his answer to it.

steps.name: Mountbatten Plan
who: Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma
steps.what: The last viceroy announced that British India would be divided into two dominions, with Punjab and Bengal split, and brought independence forward to August 1947.
steps.why: With barely ten weeks to prepare, the haste of the handover contributed to the chaos that followed.

steps.name: Independence of Pakistan
who: Louis Mountbatten, 1st Earl Mountbatten of Burma
steps.what: Mountbatten handed power to Pakistan's Constituent Assembly in Karachi, and Jinnah became governor-general of a state split into two wings 1,600 km apart.
steps.why: The Muslim League's goal of 1940 became a state.

steps.name: Tryst with Destiny
steps.what: At midnight Nehru told India's Constituent Assembly that India would 'awake to life and freedom', as it became independent with him as prime minister.
steps.why: Independence came at the same moment as partition, while Gandhi stayed in Calcutta and did not celebrate.

steps.name: Radcliffe Line
steps.what: The border drawn in five weeks by the lawyer Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India, was published two days after independence.
steps.why: Millions learned only after independence on which side of the border they lived.

steps.date_note: migrations and killings ran from August to late 1947
steps.name: Partition migrations
steps.what: About 12 to 20 million people crossed the new borders; trains of refugees were attacked in Punjab, and estimates of the dead range from several hundred thousand to two million.
steps.why: This is the human cost that made partition one of the century's great tragedies.

steps.name: Gandhi's Calcutta fast
steps.what: When riots broke out again in Calcutta, Gandhi fasted until leaders of both communities pledged to keep the peace, and the city stayed largely calm.
steps.why: It showed what moral pressure could do while Punjab burned.

steps.name: Indo-Pakistani war of 1947–1948
steps.what: After tribal fighters from Pakistan invaded Kashmir, its Hindu maharaja signed accession to India, and Indian troops were flown into Srinagar on 27 October.
steps.why: Kashmir became a divided and lasting cause of conflict between India and Pakistan.

steps.name: Assassination of Mahatma Gandhi
steps.what: Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist who blamed Gandhi for favouring Muslims and Pakistan, shot him at a prayer meeting.
steps.why: The shock helped calm communal violence in India and discredited Hindu extremists for a time.

stories.title: The Cold War's crises
stories.blurb: How did the rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union nearly lead to war, and why did it end so quietly?

steps.name: Iron Curtain speech
steps.what: Churchill told an American audience that an 'iron curtain' had descended across Europe from Stettin to Trieste.
steps.why: It gave the new division of Europe its name and urged an Anglo-American alliance against the Soviets.

steps.name: Marshall Plan
steps.what: In a Harvard speech, Secretary of State Marshall offered aid to rebuild Europe; about 13 billion dollars went to Western Europe from 1948 to 1952.
steps.why: Stalin kept Eastern Europe out, so economic aid deepened the split into two blocs.

steps.name: Berlin Blockade
steps.what: The Soviets cut road and rail links to West Berlin; American and British planes flew in about 2.3 million tons of food and coal over eleven months.
steps.why: The first Cold War crisis ended without shots and led to NATO and two German states in 1949.

steps.name: Korean War
steps.what: North Korea invaded the South; US-led UN forces and then Chinese armies joined in, and an armistice signed at Panmunjom left the border near where it began.
steps.why: The Cold War became a hot war in Asia, killing millions and leaving Korea divided.

steps.name: Hungarian Revolution of 1956
steps.what: A student protest became a national uprising; Imre Nagy announced Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact, and Soviet tanks crushed the revolt.
steps.why: The West did not intervene, showing that each side would not fight inside the other's sphere.

steps.name: Sputnik 1
steps.what: The Soviet Union launched the first artificial satellite, a 58 cm sphere that circled the Earth every 96 minutes.
steps.why: It showed Soviet rockets could reach America and began the space race.

steps.name: Construction of the Berlin Wall
steps.what: East German troops sealed the border through Berlin overnight with barbed wire, later replaced by a concrete wall.
steps.why: It stopped the flight of millions of East Germans west and became the Cold War's main symbol.

steps.name: Cuban Missile Crisis
steps.what: US spy planes found Soviet nuclear missile sites in Cuba; after a naval quarantine and 13 days of tension, Khrushchev agreed to remove them.
steps.why: It was the closest the world came to nuclear war, and led to a hotline between Washington and Moscow.

steps.name: Tet Offensive
steps.what: North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces attacked over 100 towns in South Vietnam; the battle for Huế lasted almost a month.
steps.why: Although a military defeat for the attackers, it turned American opinion against the Vietnam War.

steps.name: Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia
steps.what: About 250,000 Warsaw Pact troops entered Czechoslovakia to end Dubček's Prague Spring reforms.
steps.why: The Brezhnev Doctrine made clear Moscow would use force to keep its bloc communist.

steps.name: Helsinki Accords
steps.what: Thirty-five states, including the US and USSR, accepted Europe's postwar borders and promised to respect human rights.
steps.why: The high point of détente; dissidents in the East later used its human rights clauses against their governments.

steps.name: Soviet–Afghan War
steps.what: Soviet troops entered Afghanistan to prop up a communist government and fought a nine-year war against US-backed mujahideen.
steps.why: It ended détente and drained Soviet resources and morale.

steps.name: Gdańsk shipyard strike
steps.what: Shipyard workers led by the electrician Lech Wałęsa struck and won the right to form Solidarity, the first independent trade union in the Soviet bloc.
steps.why: A workers' movement in a workers' state challenged communist rule from below.

steps.name: Chernobyl disaster
steps.what: Reactor No. 4 exploded during a safety test, spreading radioactive fallout across Europe; over 100,000 people were evacuated.
steps.why: The early cover-up and later admissions weakened faith in the Soviet system and pushed Gorbachev's openness policy.

steps.name: Fall of the Berlin Wall
steps.what: After an official mistakenly announced that travel rules were lifted at once, crowds forced the border guards to open the crossings.
steps.why: Without Soviet tanks to stop it, communist rule in Eastern Europe collapsed within weeks, and Germany reunited in 1990.

steps.name: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
steps.what: A day after Gorbachev resigned and the red flag was lowered over the Kremlin, the Supreme Soviet voted the USSR out of existence, leaving 15 states.
steps.why: The Cold War ended with the peaceful break-up of one of the two superpowers.

stories.title: Africa's independence
stories.blurb: How did most of Africa win independence from European rule, and what came after?

steps.name: Suez Crisis
steps.what: After Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal, Israel, Britain and France invaded Egypt, then withdrew under American and Soviet pressure.
steps.why: It showed that Britain and France could no longer act as imperial powers against US wishes.

steps.name: Independence of Ghana
steps.what: The Gold Coast became Ghana, the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence, with Kwame Nkrumah as prime minister.
steps.why: Ghana became a model and a base for independence movements across the continent.

steps.name: Sharpeville massacre
steps.what: South African police opened fire on a crowd protesting the pass laws, killing 69 people.
steps.why: The ANC and PAC were banned and turned to armed struggle, while South Africa moved against the tide of independence.

steps.name: Congo Crisis
steps.what: The Belgian Congo became independent with Lumumba as prime minister; within weeks the army mutinied and Katanga seceded.
steps.why: A rushed handover drew in Belgium, the UN and both superpowers, a pattern of Cold War meddling in Africa.

steps.name: Year of Africa
steps.what: Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, became independent, one of 17 African states to do so in 1960, most of them former French colonies.
steps.why: In a single year most of the continent's colonial map was redrawn.

steps.name: Killing of Patrice Lumumba
steps.what: Deposed and handed to Katangan secessionists, Lumumba was shot by a firing squad with Belgian officers present.
steps.why: His death became a symbol of foreign interference in Africa's new states.

steps.name: Algerian independence
steps.what: After eight years of war that killed hundreds of thousands, Algeria became independent and about 800,000 European settlers left for France.
steps.why: It was the bloodiest of Africa's wars of independence and brought down France's Fourth Republic.

steps.name: Founding of the Organisation of African Unity
steps.what: Leaders of 32 independent African states founded the OAU, agreeing to respect the borders inherited from colonial rule.
steps.why: Keeping colonial borders avoided border wars but left many divided peoples inside them.

steps.name: Rivonia Trial
steps.what: Nelson Mandela and seven other ANC leaders were sentenced to life imprisonment for sabotage; Mandela was sent to Robben Island.
steps.why: Apartheid's opponents were jailed for decades, and Mandela became the world's best-known prisoner.

steps.name: Akosombo Dam
steps.what: Ghana dammed the Volta River, creating Lake Volta, one of the world's largest reservoirs, to power an aluminium smelter; about 80,000 people were resettled.
steps.why: New states bet on big projects to turn political independence into economic development.

steps.name: Nigerian Civil War
steps.what: The southeastern region declared itself the Republic of Biafra; in the war and blockade that followed, between one and two million people died, many from starvation.
steps.why: It tested whether colonial borders could hold, and images of its famine shaped modern humanitarian aid.

steps.name: Soweto uprising
steps.what: Police fired on thousands of schoolchildren protesting the forced use of Afrikaans in their schools; at least 176 people were killed.
steps.why: A new generation joined the struggle and international pressure on apartheid grew.

steps.name: Independence of Zimbabwe
steps.what: After a guerrilla war against the white minority regime of Rhodesia and the Lancaster House talks, Zimbabwe became independent under Robert Mugabe.
steps.why: Southern Africa's white-ruled states were reduced to South Africa and its Namibian territory.

steps.name: Release of Nelson Mandela
steps.what: Nine days after President de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC, Mandela walked free after 27 years in prison.
steps.why: It opened negotiations to end apartheid.

steps.name: Rwandan genocide
steps.what: Hutu extremist militias and soldiers killed about 500,000 to 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about 100 days while UN peacekeepers were withdrawn.
steps.why: The world's failure to act became a lasting reproach.

steps.name: 1994 South African general election
steps.what: In South Africa's first election open to all races, voters queued for hours; the ANC won 62 percent and Mandela became president.
steps.why: The end of apartheid closed the era of white minority rule in Africa.

stories.title: China from Mao to Deng
stories.blurb: How did the Communists win China, and how did the country move from Mao's revolutions to Deng's markets?

steps.name: Long March
steps.what: About 86,000 Red Army soldiers broke out of the Nationalist encirclement of their Jiangxi base and began a retreat that would cover about 10,000 km.
steps.why: The retreat saved the Communist movement and became its founding legend.

steps.name: Zunyi Conference
steps.what: At a party meeting in a captured town, leaders blamed the Comintern advisers for the defeats and gave Mao a leading role in military command.
steps.why: It began Mao's rise to the top of the party.

steps.name: End of the Long March
steps.what: Mao's column, reduced to about 8,000 people, reached the Communist base in northern Shaanxi after a year of marching.
steps.why: The northwest, later centred on Yan'an, became the base from which the Communists grew.

steps.name: Xi'an Incident
steps.what: The Nationalist general Zhang Xueliang detained Chiang Kai-shek until he agreed to stop fighting the Communists and unite against Japan.
steps.why: The second united front gave the Communists room to survive and expand during the war with Japan.

steps.name: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China
steps.what: After winning the civil war, Mao proclaimed the People's Republic from the Tiananmen gate; Chiang's government retreated to Taiwan in December.
steps.why: The Communist Party took control of the world's most populous country.
steps.wikipedia: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China

steps.name: Great Leap Forward
steps.what: An experimental commune merged farms in Suiping County into one huge unit; by the end of 1958 most of rural China was in people's communes with communal kitchens and backyard steel furnaces.
steps.why: Mao's plan to overtake Britain in industry within 15 years reorganised the lives of 500 million peasants.

steps.name: Great Chinese Famine
steps.what: Inflated harvest reports, grain requisitions and the collapse of farming caused famine; over a million died in Xinyang prefecture alone, and estimates nationally range from 15 to 55 million.
steps.why: It was probably the deadliest famine in history and weakened Mao's standing for a time.

steps.date_note: the Cultural Revolution was launched in May 1966
steps.name: Cultural Revolution
steps.what: Mao greeted about a million Red Guards in Tiananmen Square, the first of eight mass rallies; across China, students attacked teachers, officials and temples.
steps.why: Mao used the young to destroy his rivals in the party, at the cost of a decade of chaos and persecution.

steps.date_note: Mao's directive of 22 December 1968 began the mass movement
steps.name: Down to the Countryside Movement
steps.what: Mao ordered educated urban youth to go to the countryside to learn from peasants; about 17 million were sent to villages over the next decade.
steps.why: It ended the Red Guard phase and shaped a 'lost generation' that later included many reform-era leaders.

steps.name: 1972 visit by Richard Nixon to China
steps.what: Nixon became the first US president to visit the People's Republic, meeting Mao and signing the Shanghai Communiqué.
steps.why: China and the US lined up against the Soviet Union, and China began to come out of isolation.
steps.wikipedia: 1972 visit by Richard Nixon to China

steps.name: 1976 Tangshan earthquake
steps.what: An earthquake levelled the industrial city of Tangshan, killing at least 242,000 people by the official count; Mao died six weeks later on 9 September.
steps.why: Many Chinese saw the disaster as an omen of the end of the Mao era.

steps.name: Household responsibility system
steps.what: Eighteen farmers in Xiaogang village secretly divided the collective's land into family plots, each household keeping what it grew above its quota.
steps.why: Their harvests jumped, and the practice spread nationwide, ending the communes.

steps.name: Third plenary session of the 11th Central Committee
steps.what: The party shifted its focus from class struggle to economic modernisation, and Deng Xiaoping emerged as China's paramount leader.
steps.why: This meeting is taken as the start of reform and opening up.
steps.wikipedia: Third plenary session of the 11th Central Committee of the Chinese Communist Party

steps.name: Shenzhen Special Economic Zone
steps.what: A border town of about 30,000 people next to Hong Kong became a special economic zone open to foreign investment and market prices.
steps.why: Shenzhen became the test bed for capitalism under party rule and grew into a city of millions.

steps.name: 1989 Tiananmen Square protests and massacre
steps.what: After seven weeks of student-led protests, troops and tanks cleared central Beijing; hundreds, possibly thousands, were killed.
steps.why: The party showed it would allow economic reform but not political change.

steps.name: Deng Xiaoping's southern tour
steps.what: At 87 and holding no formal office, Deng toured Shenzhen, Zhuhai, Guangzhou and Shanghai, urging faster market reform.
steps.why: It restarted reforms stalled after 1989 and set the course for China's rapid growth.
